messages.author: 51b32f15a4e00229
messages.subject: Question about increment_log_prob()
parts:
Hi All,

In the Stan 2.2.0 manual entry on increment_log_prob(), it says:

"Vector arguments are included for convenience and have no speed advantage over adding values in a loop." (p. 266)

Is the lack of speed improvement an inherent limitation to the defining your own likelihoods or could this function be "vectorized" in a way that leads to speed improvements (like the built in distributional forms)? If the latter, is that a feature the Stan team is considering implementing?

I ask because I have a model that uses a mixture likelihood and I am in the process of speeding it up and vectorizing the likelihood seems like a place where my model could improve.

Thanks for your help and the great software.

Best,
Scott

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Question about increment_log_prob()
parts:
There's no way to speed it up because it's already optimized!

Loops are fast in Stan already, because they're just compiled to C++.

In Stan, the speed boost from vectorization comes from reducing
the size of the expression tree involved in automatic differentiation.
The increment_log_prob() function itself uses an accumulator so that
the effect of calling it multiple times stores up the value and then
produces a single node in the expression tree with all the summands
as operands.

More specifically, given an array

real foo[N];

the Stan code

for (n in 1:N)
increment_log_prob(foo[n]);

is translated to C++ as:

for (int n = 1; n <= N; ++n)
lp_accumulator.add(foo[n-1]);

where lp_accumulator is an instance of stan::math::accumulator.

In contrast, the Stan code

increment_log_prob(foo);

is translated to C++ as:

lp_accumulator.add(foo);

Now the reason they are roughly the same is that the
accumulator class is defined this way:

template <typename T>
class accumulator {
private:
std::vector<T> buf_;

...
template <typename S>
typename boost::enable_if<boost::is_arithmetic<S>, void>::type
add(S x) {
buf_.push_back(static_cast<T>(x));
}

template <typename S>
void add(const std::vector<S>& xs) {
for (size_t i = 0; i < xs.size(); ++i)
add(xs[i]);
}
...

So it works out to almost identical C++ code. There is a bit more indirection
in the vectorized call, but that'll almost certainly be inlined by the compiler.

- Bob

messages.author: cab04b8f0759c712
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Question about increment_log_prob()
parts:
I'm glad Bob responded -- I was going to write something a lot simpler.

I'll try to address one of your questions with what I think you were intending:

On Mar 12, 2014, at 9:15 PM, Scott Baldwin <baldw...@gmail.com> wrote:
> Is the lack of speed improvement an inherent limitation to the defining your own likelihoods or could this function be "vectorized" in a way that leads to speed improvements (like the built in distributional forms)?

You can "vectorize" your own likelihoods. For most MCMC algorithms, you need a function that's (multiplicatively) proportional to the joint distribution. In Stan, since we're on the log scale, that means additive proportionality. I'll try to be concrete with an example. If your model is:
data {
  int N;
  real y[N];
  real<lower=0> sigma;
}
parameters {
  real mu;
}
model {
  y ~ normal(mu, sigma);
}

That can be written equivalently as:
...
model {
  for (n in 1:N) {
    increment_log_prob(log(1));
    increment_log_prob(-log(sigma * sqrt(2 * pi());
    increment_log_prob(-square(y[n] - mu) / (2 * square(sigma)) );
  }
}

Let's start with "vectorization." If you notice, we just calculated "2 * square(sigma)" a total of N times. But we know what this is and don't need to do that. So let's save some computation and move that to the transformed data block:

transformed data {
  real C;
  C <- 1 / (2 * square(sigma));
}
model {
  for (n in 1:N) {
    increment_log_prob(log(1));
    increment_log_prob(-log(sigma * sqrt(2 * pi());
    increment_log_prob(-square(y[n] - mu) * C);
  }
}
(multiplication is faster than division -- doesn't matter so much in this model, but just pointing it out)

We just "vectorized" the calculation. We've saved a computation that would have been repeated in a loop.

Can we make this faster? Yes, we can. I mentioned earlier that you only need additive proportionality. That means you can drop any additive constant. Constant is relative to the Stan model defined -- if there's anything in an increment_log_prob() that has no expression containing a parameter or transformed parameter, we get to drop it. That expresses the same model! It makes the model go faster because of reasons Bob's mentioned with respect to our autodiff.

In the model, that means we can drop these lines:
- increment_log_prob(log(1));
- increment_log_prob(-log(sigma * sqrt(2 * pi());
The first one should be obvious. We're just incrementing by 0.
The second line is where we've done some cool things under the hood with Stan. When you use Stan's distribution function, we automatically drop that term because sigma is defined as data, 2 and pi() are obviously constants, so the log of that is constant **with respect to the model defined**. If sigma were defined as a parameter, you would need to keep this term.

So the final model that will approach Stan's speed will look like:
data {
  int N;
  real y[N];
  real<lower=0> sigma;
}
ransformed data {
  real C;
  C <- 1 / (2 * square(sigma));
}
model {
  for (n in 1:N) {
    increment_log_prob(-square(y[n] - mu) * C);
  }
}


(I think that was what you were getting at. If not, hopefully that was insightful anyway.)



Daniel

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Question about increment_log_prob()
parts:
On Mar 12, 2014, at 10:16 PM, Daniel Lee <bea...@alum.mit.edu> wrote:

...

> So the final model that will approach Stan's speed will look like:
> data {
> int N;
> real y[N];
> real<lower=0> sigma;
> }

> transformed data {
> real C;
> C <- 1 / (2 * square(sigma));
> }
> model {
> for (n in 1:N) {

And then you can go one better in terms of size and speed
by using our efficient dot_self function with y declared
as a vector (and including mu as a parameter, which I think
is what we're estimating?):

data {
int<lower=0> N;
vector[N] y;

increment_log_prob(-0.5 * dot_self(y - mu) / square(sigma));
}

You can do the same thing for defining the MLE for the coefficients
and variance in a linear regression using Stan's optimizer:

data {
int<lower=0> N;
int<lower=1> K;
vector[N] y;
matrix[N,K] x;
}
parameters {
vector[K] beta;
}
transformed parameters {
real<lower=0> squared_error;
squared_error <- dot_self(y - x * beta);
}
model {
increment_log_prob(-squared_error);
}
generated quantities {
real<lower=0> sigma_squared;
sigma_squared <- squared_error / N;
}

This assumes a column in x of all 1s for an intercept; otherwise
you can add an intercept parameter real beta; and replace
(y - x * beta) with y - (alpha + x * beta).

That's the MLE for variance (sigma_squared), but you can replace the
denominator N with (N - K) [or N - K - 1 if you include a separate
intercept] and get the more standard unbiased estimate of variance.

Stan's optimizer if faster than the lm() function built into R
as the matrix of predictors and number of parameters gets into the
thousands, and we've barely even begun to think about optimizing
the optimizer's code :-)

- Bob
